newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Pru says in no rush to buy.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Pru says in no rush to buy.

text.p: Prudential Corp is in no rush to buy a building society or life assurer following the sale of its M&G reinsurance operation for a bigger than expected 1.75 billion stg, said Prudential group chief executive Peter Davis.
"We certainly won't be rushed into doing something simply because we now have greater availability of funds," Davis told Reuters in an interview.

"If the right opportunity presents itself at a sensible price and we can demonstrate value to our shareholders, then we'll do it," he said, but added the pace of change in the life assurance industry and among mutual building societies was slow.
Davis declined to comment on whether Prudential, Britain's biggest life and pensions provider, was in talks with any building societies or life assurers about merging.
The group earlier on Tuesday said it was selling M&G to Swiss Reinsurance, following an announcement in June that it intended to float a substantial part of the operation.
Swiss Re had been in the running to buy U.S. property and casualty reinsurer American Re, which was bought by Munich Re earlier this month for $3.3 billion.
M&G is mainly a life and health reinsurer, but with a global presence and net assets of 1.1 billion stg at the end of 1995.

Davis said he believed Prudential had secured a higher price than expected for M&G because, as one of the top specialist life and health reinsurers worldwide, it was in a less volatile area of the global reinsurance industry than a general reinsurer.
"It was attractive to a number of bidders," he said, while declining to specify how many companies had been interested.

Prudential had been pursuing in parallel the possible flotation of M&G, particularly through the U.S. market, which Davis said has experience of valuing reinsurance companies in a way that London does not.
"It was always a serious intention of ours to float the M&G, unless one of the trade buyers particularly wanted to buy it."

"But with a limited number of buyers and with other rationalisation going on, the timing might not have been right or someone may already have done something else. So we were always pursuing a twin track approach," said Davis. -- Christopher Adams, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 7721
